desc:
The array nums is a permutation of the integers 1 to n. You are also given a list of smaller sequences sequences; each one lists distinct values from 1..n.

Consider all arrangements (permutations) of 1..n in which every sequence appears as a subsequence, that is, its values occur in that relative order (not necessarily next to each other). Return true if nums is such an arrangement and it is the only one; otherwise return false. If no arrangement exists at all, the answer is false.

nums = [1,2,3], sequences = [[1,2],[2,3]]  -> true
nums = [1,2,3], sequences = [[1,2],[1,3]]  -> false   ([1,3,2] also works)
nums = [1,2,3], sequences = [[1,2]]        -> false   (3 can go anywhere)
nums = [1,2],   sequences = [[1,2],[2,1]]  -> false   (contradiction)
nums = [3,1,2], sequences = [[3,1,2]]      -> true
constraints: 0 ≤ sequences.length ≤ 3,000; each sequence has between 1 and n values, distinct inside the sequence, in [1, n]
The total length of all sequences is at most 8,000
hints: Every sequence only says 'x comes before y' for neighbouring values. Turn each neighbouring pair into a directed edge.
An arrangement that respects all sequences is a topological order of that graph. So the question is whether the graph has exactly one topological order, and whether it is nums.

Run Kahn's algorithm and look at the queue. If at any moment two or more nodes have indegree 0, they could be placed in either order, so the answer is false. Otherwise compare each removed node with the next value of nums, and finally check that all n nodes were removed (a cycle leaves some behind).
editorial: A sequence is a subsequence of an arrangement exactly when each neighbouring pair of the sequence appears in the right order (order is transitive), so only the pairs (s[i], s[i+1]) matter. Build a directed graph on 1..n from those pairs; the valid arrangements are precisely the topological orders of this graph.

A DAG has a unique topological order exactly when, at every step of Kahn's algorithm, there is only one node with indegree 0: if two were available, swapping them would give a second order, and if one is always available there is never a choice. So run Kahn's algorithm, return false as soon as the set of ready nodes has size other than 1, or when the node removed differs from nums[i].

At the end the number of removed nodes must be n. If a cycle exists (contradicting sequences) the ready set becomes empty before n nodes are removed, which also gives false. Values missing from every sequence start with indegree 0 and would be ready at the same time as another node (unless n = 1), correctly producing false. Repeated pairs must be counted once, so use a set per node or deduplicate. Time and space are O(n + total length).
